newsitem.title: USA: Chicago mayor plans $1 bln bonds for neighborhoods.
newsitem.headline: Chicago mayor plans $1 bln bonds for neighborhoods.

text.p: Chicago Mayor Richard Daley has proposed $1 billion of bonds for neighborhood improvements over the next three years.
In a state of the city address Wednesday night, Daley announced that Chicago has invested $1 billion in its neighborhoods since 1990 and will match that total by 2000.
In the first year, as announced by Daley last week, changes in the pension fund systems would finance $200 million of bonds for the program he has dubbed "Neighborhoods Alive."

The changes, which need legislative approval, would also allow for a $20 million property tax cut and help pave the way for the elimination of the city's "head tax" levy on businesses that have more than 50 employees.

Daley has proposed to reduce the funding in two of the city's five employee pension funds in order to provide additional support in the funds for firefighters and police officers and money for the capital improvement plan.
Currently, two funds hold more than 100 percent of their liabilities, while the police and fire pension funds can cover barely 50 percent of their anticipated liabilities.
The Daley proposal would seek to boost those two funds to a 70 percent level, while not reducing the relative strength of the other funds, city officials have said.
But critics of the Daley proposal call the plan a raid on the pension funds and question whether it would reduce their financial stability.
The "Neighborhoods Alive" program would pay for resurfacing 4,200 city blocks, building 124 blocks of new streets and paving 321 new alleys. Another 4,300 alleys would be resurfaced.
